subject: Cognitive Science
title: Ambiguity Resolution
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Ambiguity Resolution.

hook.text: 'I saw her duck.' Did she crouch, or do you see her pet? Your brain resolves this in milliseconds.

buildup.text: Most words are ambiguous. 'Bank' has over ten meanings. But in context, you rarely even notice.

discovery.text: Research shows your brain briefly activates all meanings of an ambiguous word—then suppresses the wrong ones.

twist.text: Patients with right hemisphere damage can't suppress the wrong meanings. They get derailed by puns and double meanings.

climax.text: Context is king. The sentence, the paragraph, and the world knowledge around a word steer the brain's choice.

punchline.text: You hear a word, activate many meanings, and kill all but one.

quiz.question: What does the brain first do when encountering an ambiguous word?

details.summary: Most words and sentences are ambiguous, yet comprehension feels effortless. The word bank has multiple meanings; context rapidly selects the right one. Ambiguity resolution relies on frequency, context, and world knowledge, and it happens within milliseconds of encountering the ambiguous item.
details.whyItMatters: Ambiguity resolution is the central problem of language comprehension. That we solve it so quickly and unconsciously reveals the power of the language processing system.
takeaways: Most words have multiple meanings that context resolves
Dominant meanings are accessed first regardless of context
Resolution occurs within hundreds of milliseconds

faq.question: Are all meanings of a word activated simultaneously?
faq.answer: Initially yes. Research shows that both meanings of an ambiguous word like bank are briefly activated, even when context strongly favors one. Within a few hundred milliseconds, the inappropriate meaning is suppressed. This brief multiple activation followed by selection is well-established.

faq.question: What makes some ambiguities harder to resolve?
faq.answer: Balanced ambiguities where both meanings are equally frequent are harder than biased ones. Ambiguity across syntactic categories, like rose as noun or verb, is resolved differently from within-category ambiguity. Distant or weak contextual cues also slow resolution and increase processing cost.
